question: Which ONE combination of findings BEST satisfies the paediatric definition of fulminant hepatic failure (FHF)?

answers.text: Jaundice for 4 weeks with AST 300 U/L and ALT 280 U/L in a child with known chronic hepatitis B.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. This child has chronic liver disease (known hepatitis B). FHF is defined specifically as occurring WITHOUT pre-existing liver disease. An acute decompensation in a known CLD patient is 'acute-on-chronic liver failure', a distinct entity.

answers.text: Hepatic encephalopathy (drowsy, confused) + INR 2.2 developing within 8 weeks in a previously healthy 7-year-old with no prior liver disease.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. FHF in children = hepatic encephalopathy + coagulopathy (INR >1.5, no Vitamin K correction) within 8 weeks of onset, in a patient without prior liver disease. In India, the commonest causes in children are HAV, HEV, Wilson disease (presenting as acute liver failure), drug-induced (paracetamol, anti-TB drugs), and indeterminate. Wilson disease FHF classically shows paradoxically LOW alkaline phosphatase — a key diagnostic clue.

answers.text: Total bilirubin of 18 mg/dL with pruritus and pale stools in a 2-year-old presenting at 6 weeks of age.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. This describes neonatal cholestasis (conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia presenting at 6 weeks) — a separate diagnostic category. The differential includes biliary atresia (requires Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days of life), Alagille syndrome, progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, and metabolic causes. It does NOT fulfil the criteria for FHF.

answers.text: AST 800 U/L, ALT 650 U/L, and jaundice in a child who is alert, eating well, and has an INR of 1.2.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Very elevated transaminases with jaundice but no encephalopathy and INR <1.5 = severe acute hepatitis, NOT FHF. The defining features of FHF are ENCEPHALOPATHY + COAGULOPATHY. Transaminase elevation alone, however extreme, does not define FHF.

overallFeedback.feedback: FHF definition: (1) encephalopathy AND (2) coagulopathy (INR >1.5) within 8 weeks AND (3) no pre-existing liver disease. Elevated transaminases alone ≠ FHF. Known CLD with decompensation ≠ FHF. Wilson disease FHF: paradoxically LOW ALP is the signature clue.

Correct. FHF = encephalopathy + INR >1.5 within 8 weeks without prior liver disease. Wilson disease FHF has a distinctive clue: LOW (paradoxically low) alkaline phosphatase despite severe liver injury, due to haemolysis consuming Zn-containing ALP. Always check serum copper/ceruloplasmin in a child with unexplained FHF.
